Name: OpenAPI Code Generation
Strategy: Generate server stubs and client SDKs from OpenAPI/Swagger specification
Tooling: OpenAPI Generator; Swagger Codegen; oapi-codegen (Go); openapi-typescript
Strengths: Single source of truth; auto-generated clients reduce bugs; documentation always in sync
Weaknesses: Generated code can be hard to customize; spec drift if not enforced in CI; boilerplate overhead
When to Use: Teams with multiple client platforms consuming the same API; public APIs with external consumers
Gotcha: Generated code must be treated as build artifact not checked in — regenerate on every spec change

Name: GraphQL Federation
Strategy: Compose multiple GraphQL subgraphs into a single unified supergraph via a gateway
Tooling: Apollo Federation; GraphQL Mesh; Grafbase; WunderGraph
Strengths: Teams own their subgraphs independently; unified schema for clients; declarative composition
Weaknesses: Gateway is a single point of failure; query planning complexity; cross-subgraph joins are expensive
When to Use: Microservices architectures where each team owns a domain with its own schema
Gotcha: @key directives must be planned carefully — a bad entity design creates N+1 queries across subgraphs

Name: Schema Evolution (Backward Compatible)
Strategy: Evolve API schema by only making additive non-breaking changes
Tooling: Buf (protobuf); Spectral (OpenAPI); custom CI lint rules; Atlas (SQL)
Strengths: No breaking changes means no version management; clients upgrade at their own pace
Weaknesses: Can't remove or rename fields; schema grows monotonically; deprecated fields linger
When to Use: APIs with many consumers who can't coordinate upgrades; long-lived public APIs
Gotcha: Mark deprecated fields explicitly with sunset dates; monitor usage of deprecated fields before removal

Name: API Versioning via URL Path
Strategy: Version in URL path: /v1/users and /v2/users — route to different handlers
Strengths: Simple to understand; easy to route; clear separation; works with CDN caching
Weaknesses: Duplicated handlers; version sprawl; URL pollution; hard to share code between versions
When to Use: Public APIs with external consumers who need stability guarantees
Gotcha: Don't version internal APIs — use schema evolution instead; versioning is for external contracts

Name: API Versioning via Headers
Strategy: Version in Accept header: Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2
Strengths: Clean URLs; supports content negotiation; multiple versions on same path
Weaknesses: Harder to test (need headers); not cacheable by default (Vary header needed); less discoverable
When to Use: APIs where URL aesthetics matter; APIs with sophisticated clients
Gotcha: CDN caching requires Vary: Accept header — which can reduce cache hit rate dramatically

Name: Contract Testing
Strategy: Verify API contracts between consumer and provider are maintained across changes
Tooling: Pact; Spring Cloud Contract; Dredd; Schemathesis; Specmatic
Strengths: Catches breaking changes before deployment; consumer-driven; decouples teams
Weaknesses: Setup overhead; contract maintenance burden; requires both sides to participate
When to Use: Microservices with many inter-service API calls; organizations with independent team deployments
Gotcha: Consumer-driven contracts test what consumers actually use not the full API — dead endpoints stay untested

Name: Protobuf Schema Registry
Strategy: Centralized registry for protobuf schemas with compatibility enforcement
Tooling: Buf Schema Registry; Confluent Schema Registry (protobuf); custom registries
Strengths: Backward/forward compatibility checks; schema discovery; breaking change prevention
Weaknesses: Infrastructure to maintain; learning curve for teams new to protobuf; migration from JSON is effort
When to Use: gRPC-based microservices; Kafka with protobuf serialization; teams needing strict schema governance
Gotcha: Protobuf field numbers are forever — never reuse a field number; use reserved to prevent accidents

Name: AsyncAPI for Event-Driven APIs
Strategy: Specification format for documenting async/event-driven APIs analogous to OpenAPI for REST
Strengths: Standardized event documentation; code generation for consumers; protocol agnostic
Weaknesses: Tooling less mature than OpenAPI; adoption still growing; not all brokers supported equally
When to Use: Event-driven architectures with Kafka/RabbitMQ/WebSocket that need documentation and client generation
Gotcha: AsyncAPI 3.0 is a breaking change from 2.x — check tooling support before upgrading spec version

Name: BFF (Backend for Frontend) Pattern
Strategy: Dedicated API layer per frontend that aggregates and transforms backend service calls
Tooling: Custom services; Apollo Server; tRPC; GraphQL as BFF
Strengths: Optimized payloads per client; decouples frontend from backend service topology; team autonomy
Weaknesses: Multiple BFFs to maintain; risk of duplicated business logic; latency from aggregation layer
When to Use: Multi-platform products (web + mobile + third-party); teams with distinct frontend/backend ownership
Gotcha: BFF should only aggregate and transform — business logic in BFF is the path to a distributed monolith

Name: API Gateway Pattern
Strategy: Centralized entry point for all API calls — authentication and rate limiting and routing
Tooling: Kong; AWS API Gateway; Envoy; Traefik; APISIX; Tyk
Strengths: Centralized cross-cutting concerns; simplified client interaction; security enforcement at edge
Weaknesses: Single point of failure; latency overhead; configuration complexity; can become a bottleneck
When to Use: Any API with multiple backend services; when you need centralized auth and rate limiting and logging
Gotcha: API gateway should be dumb routing — putting business logic in the gateway creates coupling and deployment bottlenecks

Name: gRPC-Web
Strategy: Enable gRPC calls from browser clients via an Envoy proxy or grpc-web protocol
Tooling: grpc-web; Envoy gRPC-Web filter; Connect (from Buf)
Strengths: Strongly typed browser-to-backend; shared protobuf types; streaming support (server-side)
Weaknesses: Requires proxy; no bidirectional streaming in browsers; debugging harder than REST; tooling gaps
When to Use: Full-stack teams using protobuf who want type consistency from browser to backend
Gotcha: Browser gRPC only supports unary and server-streaming — bidirectional streaming requires WebSocket fallback

Name: Hypermedia APIs (HATEOAS)
Strategy: API responses include links to related resources and available actions
Tooling: Spring HATEOAS; HAL; JSON:API; Siren; custom link headers
Strengths: Self-documenting; client doesn't hardcode URLs; evolvable API design
Weaknesses: Verbose responses; complex client implementation; rarely implemented fully in practice
When to Use: Public APIs where discoverability matters; APIs that need to evolve without breaking clients
Gotcha: HATEOAS is theoretically elegant but practically rare — most teams get more value from good documentation + OpenAPI
